title: Code of Hammurabi stele
summary: A basalt stele 225 cm tall, inscribed with 282 laws and topped by a relief of the god Shamash and Hammurabi, belongs to the reign of Hammurabi of Babylon (1792–1750 BCE, per the Louvre). It was found broken at Susa in 1901–1902 and is now in the Louvre. World History Encyclopedia says an Elamite king probably carried it off from Sippar around 1150 BCE.

uncertainty.note: Dated c. 1754 BCE in one photo caption and around 1750 BCE in the same article (ParisToVersailles); the Louvre dates it to Hammurabi's reign, 1792–1750 BCE (astronomical -1791 to -1749), so the start could be up to about 38 years earlier. World History Encyclopedia says the code may date to circa 1722 BCE or later, and lists c. 1772 BCE in its timeline.

as_recorded.calendar: BCE, First Dynasty of Babylon, reign of Hammurabi

where.modern_name: Susa (Shush), Iran: findspot of the stele; the stele is now in the Louvre, Paris
where.historical_name: Susa, an Elamite city, where the stele was found; made in Babylonia (the Louvre gives 'Iraq = Mesopotamia'), original site not stated

importance.justification: One of the earliest and best preserved Mesopotamian law texts, displayed as a public stele.

sources.title: The Complete Guide to the Code of Hammurabi at the Louvre

reviewer_note: Pinned at Susa (findspot), not the Louvre and not Babylon: the Louvre record gives only Mesopotamia as place of creation. The 1754 BCE date rests on one travel-guide caption; the Louvre gives only the reign, and World History Encyclopedia contradicts itself (1722 vs 1772).
